title: Adani's Mumbai Airport Duty-Free Shops Were Caught Selling Illegal Nicotine Pouches. The Court Case Could Reshape Airport Regulation Across India.
excerpt: An Indian government investigation found unapproved nicotine products on sale in the departure zone at South Asia's busiest international airport — and Adani is arguing the law doesn't apply
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Mumbai airport duty-free shops sold illegal nicotine pouches, prompting a government investigation.
  • Adani Group argues that drug regulations shouldn't apply to duty-free outlets.
  • Nicotine pouches are unapproved in India, raising public health concerns among young adults.
  • A court ruling could reshape airport regulations and affect Adani's retail operations.
  • Duty-free shopping rituals for NRIs may involve illegal products under Indian law.

Source: Reuters
An Indian government investigation has found that duty-free shops at Mumbai's international airport — run by a joint venture led by Gautam Adani's business group — were selling nicotine pouches in breach of the law, according to documents reviewed by Reuters. The case could set a legal precedent that reshapes how India regulates one of the world's fastest-growing tobacco alternatives at airports across the country. The discovery strikes at a gap in India's regulatory framework that millions of NRI travellers pass through every year: the airport duty-free zone. ## What the Investigation Found India's drug department inspected departure-zone duty-free shops at Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj International Airport in March, acting on complaints from the anti-nicotine advocacy group Mothers Against Vaping. Inspectors found imported nicotine pouches being sold without the registration certificates or import licences required under Indian law, government documents show. "Nicotine pouches also fall under the definition of a drug ... a valid registration certificate and import licence are mandatory," an assistant drugs controller wrote in an April letter to the airport's customs authority, attaching what the government described as an "investigation report." The shops are operated by Mumbai Travel Retail, a joint venture led by the Adani Group with Dubai-based Flemingo International. The company was directed to discontinue sales of nicotine pouches and seek the necessary approvals. ![Mumbai Airport — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8e/Chhatrapati_Shivaji_International_Airport_3.jpg/3840px-Chhatrapati_Shivaji_International_Airport_3.jpg) > **"A government study published in June described nicotine pouches as "a new and largely unregulated public health concern," flagging widespread illegal sales and consumption among Indians aged 18 to 40."** The Adani Group has denied wrongdoing and is fighting back in court. In legal filings reviewed by Reuters, the group is asking judges to declare that the Drugs and Cosmetics Act does not apply to duty-free outlets or to nicotine pouches — an argument that lawyers say, if successful, would create a regulatory carve-out for airports that could apply nationwide. ## A Public Health Flashpoint The legal battle arrives at a moment when nicotine pouches are emerging as a serious public health concern in India. Unlike traditional chewing tobacco, these small, flavoured sachets are placed between the gum and lip, delivering nicotine without smoke. They have exploded in popularity globally, particularly among younger adults. India banned e-cigarettes outright in 2019 and regulates nicotine replacement products like patches and chewing gum under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act. Nicotine pouches occupy a grey area — the government considers them unapproved and illegal, but enforcement has been patchy. A government study published in June described nicotine pouches as "a new and largely unregulated public health concern," flagging widespread illegal sales and consumption among Indians aged 18 to 40. Tobacco already kills an estimated 1.35 million people in India every year — more than the population of many mid-sized Indian cities. ## The Duty-Free Loophole At the heart of the legal dispute is a question that has never been definitively answered in Indian law: do the same drug regulations that govern shops on Indian soil apply to duty-free outlets inside airport terminals? Adani's legal team argues they do not. The group contends that duty-free zones operate under customs supervision and that products sold there are technically in transit — not entering the Indian domestic market. If the courts agree, it would establish that airport duty-free shops exist in a regulatory no-man's land where products banned or unapproved on Indian streets can be freely sold to departing passengers. ![Gautam Adani — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/ff/Gautam_Adani.jpg) Public health lawyers counter that the passengers buying these products are overwhelmingly Indian citizens or residents. "The fiction that a duty-free shop is somehow outside India when it sits inside an Indian airport is precisely that — a fiction," said one health law expert who advises the government but was not authorised to speak publicly.
The Duty-Free Dilemma
›Duty-free shops operate under customs supervision.
›Nicotine pouches are illegal under Indian law.
›Adani's legal argument could create a regulatory loophole.
›Public health advocates warn of potential health risks.
A precedent-setting government win could block the sale of nicotine pouches across all Indian airports and potentially affect other product categories sold in duty-free zones without full regulatory clearance. ## Why NRI Travellers Should Pay Attention For the millions of Indian diaspora members who transit Mumbai's airport every year — the busiest in South Asia by international passenger traffic — the case has practical implications. Duty-free shopping is a ritual for many NRIs, and the products available in the departure lounge may look familiar from shops in New York, London, or Dubai. But what is legal in a duty-free shop at Heathrow or Dubai International may not be legal at CSIA. Nicotine pouches, brands like Zyn and Velo that are widely available in the United States and Europe, are unapproved drugs under Indian law. Travellers who purchase them in the Mumbai departure lounge — or worse, carry them into India on arrival — risk running afoul of regulations they may not know exist. The case also spotlights the Adani Group's expanding airport empire. The conglomerate operates eight airports across India and has positioned its airport retail business as a growth engine. A ruling that duty-free shops must comply with the same drug regulations as domestic retailers could ripple through its retail operations at every terminal. ## What Happens Next The matter is now before the courts, where Adani's challenge to the Drugs and Cosmetics Act's applicability will be heard. The government has already directed the shops to halt nicotine pouch sales while the case proceeds. Neither the Indian health ministry nor Flemingo International responded to Reuters' requests for comment. For India's 1.35 million annual tobacco-related deaths, the legal outcome carries weight beyond airport retail. If the courts rule that duty-free zones are exempt from drug regulation, it would create a precedent that could be exploited for other unapproved health products — a gap that public health advocates are determined to close before it opens. *Sources: Reuters, Press Information Bureau (India), Drugs and Cosmetics Act documentation*
